canonicalName: Kirchhoff's circuit laws and the graph-theoretic treatment of networks
phases: Network equations solved through the branch structure (1847)

milestones.label: Ohm's galvanische Kette
milestones.work: G. S. Ohm, Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet, Berlin 1827
milestones.description: Ohm's law for single conductors supplies the current-voltage relation that Kirchhoff's network laws extend.

evidence.claim: Crossref record for the 1827 book Die galvanische Kette.
Internet Archive scan of the 1827 book.

milestones.label: Kirchhoff's paper on current through a plane
milestones.work: Kirchhoff, Ueber den Durchgang eines elektrischen Stromes durch eine Ebene, insbesondere durch eine kreisförmige, Annalen der Physik (Poggendorff) 64, 1845
milestones.description: History pages date the announcement of the current and voltage laws to 1845, the year of this paper by Kirchhoff, then a student at Königsberg.

evidence.claim: Crossref confirms a Kirchhoff paper of 1845 in Annalen der Physik (Crossref lists it as vol. 140, pp. 497-514)
MacTutor says Kirchhoff announced his laws for multi-loop circuits in 1845 while studying with Neumann
Wikipedia states the laws were first described in 1845 by Kirchhoff, generalising Ohm

milestones.note: The year of the paper is bibliographically confirmed; that this particular paper is where the two laws are first stated rests on the history pages (I did not read the paper). Later practice cites the 1847 paper for the network form.

milestones.phase: Network equations solved through the branch structure (1847)
milestones.label: Kirchhoff solves linear current distributions in networks
milestones.work: Kirchhoff, Ueber die Auflösung der Gleichungen, auf welche man bei der Untersuchung der linearen Vertheilung galvanischer Ströme geführt wird, Annalen der Physik (Poggendorff) 72, 497-508, 1847
milestones.description: Kirchhoff treated the system of equations for currents in a network of linear conductors in general; later graph theory reads this paper as an early use of the branch structure of a network (loops, trees, cyclomatic number).

evidence.claim: Crossref record for the 1847 paper, title concerning the solution of the equations for linear distribution of galvanic currents (Crossref lists vol. 148, pp. 497-508)
Wikipedia calls Kirchhoff's 1845 work the first example of modern algebra used in graph theory
Wikipedia notes that the cyclomatic number was named by Kirchhoff before Betti's paper

milestones.note: The spanning-tree (matrix-tree) content usually attributed to this paper is standard in the literature but I did not read the paper; the evidence confirms only its existence, year and subject. Wikipedia dates the algebraic graph use to 1845, the MacTutor/Crossref chain points to 1845-47.

milestones.label: Maxwell's Treatise treats networks
milestones.work: J. C. Maxwell, A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, Oxford 1873
milestones.description: Maxwell's Treatise includes a systematic account of conduction in linear networks with loop currents, building on Kirchhoff.

evidence.claim: zbMATH (Jahrbuch) record of the 1873 Treatise.
MacTutor biography of Maxwell.

milestones.note: That the Treatise discusses network loops is recalled from standard history; not read in this pass.

milestones.label: 'Note on network theory' (earliest zbMATH title with the phrase in the 1845-1950 window)
milestones.work: J. G. Brainerd, 'Note on network theory', journal article, pages 1660-1664, zbMATH record 3006808, 1932
milestones.description: The earliest title found in the searched window that uses the phrase 'network theory' for the field that Kirchhoff's circuit laws started.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record gives title 'Note on network theory', author J. G. Brainerd, year 1932, journal article, pages 1660-1664

milestones.note: Only a title-phrase lead: zbMATH coverage of 1845-1931 is partial and the journal name was not extracted; a naming role needs a stronger check before use. Kirchhoff (1845, 1847) is the event itself and is not repeated here.

works.whyItMatters: Date given for the first statement of the circuit laws

works.citation: Kirchhoff, Ueber die Auflösung der Gleichungen ... linearen Vertheilung galvanischer Ströme, Ann. Phys. 1847
works.whyItMatters: Treats the general network system and underlies the later graph-theoretic reading

people.roleNote: author of the circuit laws and the network equations

people.name: Georg Ohm

works.whyItMatters: Ohm's law, the basic relation behind Kirchhoff's network laws.

people.roleNote: predecessor whose law for one conductor Kirchhoff generalised

works.citation: A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism
works.whyItMatters: Presents circuit laws within Maxwell electromagnetic theory.

notes: Short record. The two Kirchhoff papers are bibliographically confirmed (Crossref) but their contents were not read; the claims about content rest on MacTutor and Wikipedia. Searched: Wikipedia leads (no candidate for this event), Wikipedia 'Kirchhoff's circuit laws', 'Graph theory', 'Betti number', 'Kirchhoff's theorem' (no dated history section), MacTutor biography of Kirchhoff (1845, 1847), Crossref. Not established: when the laws were first expressed in the language of graphs (nodes, branches, trees). Maxwell's 1873 Treatise (archive.org holds the edition) is a likely consolidation of the network treatment but its content was not read, so it is kept out of the milestones. No naming or institution milestone found for 'network theory'. Thin pass 2: only a few dated milestones exist in the sources read (Ohm 1827 precursor, Maxwell 1873). The graph-theoretic reading of the 1847 paper (spanning trees) rests on Wikipedia pages cited in the existing record. Later graph-theory uptake (Poincare, Veblen) was not researched.

phases: Euler and the geometry of position
Networks and trees: Kirchhoff and Cayley
The word 'graph' and the first textbook

milestones.phase: Euler and the geometry of position
milestones.label: Euler's Königsberg bridge paper
milestones.work: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, 1736 (presented)
milestones.description: Euler solved the seven-bridges problem and generalised it to a parity condition on vertex degrees, a paper that history pages regard as the first in graph theory.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia calls Euler's 1736 paper the first paper in the history of graph theory
MacTutor dates the first beginnings of topology to this 1736 paper and states its degree-parity criterion

milestones.note: The year is the date commonly given for the paper; its printing came later and I did not check the volume. The 'first' is the usual textbook attribution; no graph vocabulary exists yet.

milestones.phase: Networks and trees: Kirchhoff and Cayley
milestones.label: Kirchhoff's network equations
milestones.work: Kirchhoff, Ueber die Auflösung der Gleichungen ... galvanischer Ströme, Ann. Phys. 1847
milestones.description: An electrical engineering problem is analysed through the loop and branch structure of the network, which graph-theory histories count as the first use of modern algebra on graph-like structures.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of the 1847 paper
Wikipedia says the first example of algebraic techniques applied to graphs is Kirchhoff's work on circuit laws

milestones.note: Use of graph structure for a target problem outside pure combinatorics; the paper content itself was not read. Treated as the earliest application of the graph viewpoint, not as the start of the subject.

milestones.label: De Morgan's letter on the colouring of maps
milestones.work: De Morgan to Hamilton, letter of 23 October 1852
milestones.description: A student's question about colouring map regions reached De Morgan, who wrote it to Hamilton the same day; this private letter is the first record of the four colour problem, later reformulated for graphs.

evidence.claim: MacTutor describes the letter and its date, naming Francis Guthrie as the source of the question
Wikipedia gives 1852 and De Morgan's letter to Hamilton as the first written record

milestones.note: Private letter, so a precursor; the first public statement is handled in event H52.

milestones.phase: Networks and trees: Kirchhoff and Cayley
milestones.label: Cayley's theory of trees
milestones.work: Cayley, On the theory of the analytical forms called trees, Philosophical Magazine 13, 172-176, 1857
milestones.description: Cayley introduced rooted trees as a way to count analytic forms from the differential calculus, starting enumerative graph theory that he later tied to chemistry.

evidence.claim: Crossref record: Cayley 1857, Phil. Mag. 13, 172-176
Wikipedia describes Cayley's study of trees and its link with chemical composition as the start of enumerative graph theory

milestones.note: Cayley's 1874 paper on the mathematical theory of isomers (Phil. Mag. 47, 444-447; Crossref 10.1080/14786447408641058) carries the chemistry link but is not a separate milestone.

milestones.phase: The word 'graph' and the first textbook
milestones.label: Sylvester coins 'graph'
milestones.work: Sylvester, Chemistry and algebra, Nature 17, 284, 1878
milestones.description: Sylvester introduced the word 'graph' by analogy between invariants and chemical diagrams; the longer companion paper appeared in the American Journal of Mathematics the same year.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia attributes the term to Sylvester's 1878 Nature note
Crossref record of the Nature note (vol. 17, p. 284)
Crossref record of Sylvester, On an application of the new atomic theory ..., Am. J. Math. 1, 64 (1878)

milestones.phase: The word 'graph' and the first textbook
milestones.label: König's first textbook
milestones.work: Kőnig, Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen, Akademische Verlagsgesellschaft, Leipzig, 1936
milestones.description: The first book devoted to graph theory, combining the scattered results of the previous century.

evidence.claim: zbMATH lists the 1936 edition of Kőnig's Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen
Wikipedia calls Kőnig's 1936 book the first textbook on graph theory

works.citation: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, 1736
works.whyItMatters: Regarded as the first paper in graph theory

works.citation: Kirchhoff, Ueber die Auflösung der Gleichungen ..., Ann. Phys. 1847
works.whyItMatters: Early use of algebra on graph structure

people.roleNote: applied the branch structure of a network to current equations

notes: The input summary credits Kirchhoff's circuit trees, Cayley's tree counting and the four colour problem; sources confirm all three but Euler 1736 is the usual 'first paper' and is added as the public start. The 1852 four colour letter is private, hence a precursor here (the four colour problem has its own event). Kőnig 1936: the archive.org copies in my search are dated 1950 (reprint), so the 1936 year relies on zbMATH. Vandermonde 1771 and Listing 1847 are mentioned by Wikipedia as predecessors but not included. Not found: a journal, chair or MSC code naming graph theory.

canonicalName: Kirkman's schoolgirl problem and combinatorial designs

milestones.label: Woolhouse's questions in the Lady's and Gentleman's Diary
milestones.work: Woolhouse, question on combinations with no repeated sub-combination, The Lady's and Gentleman's Diary, 1844 (and a triad version in 1846)
milestones.description: Woolhouse's questions asked how many triads can be formed from n symbols with no pair repeated, which is the triple-system problem Kirkman then solved.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia's timeline gives Woolhouse's 1844 general question and 1846 triad question
MacTutor says Kirkman's first paper answered a problem from the Diary of 1845

milestones.note: The sources disagree on the year of the Diary question (1844/1846 versus 1845); I did not see the Diary. Kept as a precursor only.

milestones.label: Kirkman's paper on triple systems
milestones.work: Kirkman, On a problem in combinations, Cambridge and Dublin Mathematical Journal 2, 191-204, 1847
milestones.description: Kirkman fully treated the construction of systems of triples in which each pair occurs once, for orders congruent to 1 or 3 mod 6, six years before Steiner posed the question.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia dates the paper to 1847 (vol. 2, pp. 191-204) and describes it as comprehensive
Internet Archive holds the Cambridge and Dublin Mathematical Journal vol. 2 dated 1847
MacTutor says Kirkman solved the Steiner-triple problem six years before Steiner (the paper was presented in 1846)

milestones.note: Crossref, zbMATH and Open Library were searched and do not index this paper. The Internet Archive record confirms the journal volume and year only; pages and content are from Wikipedia.

milestones.label: The fifteen schoolgirls problem and its first solutions
milestones.work: Kirkman, Query VI, The Lady's and Gentleman's Diary, 1850; Kirkman, On the triads made with fifteen things, Philosophical Magazine 37, 169-171, 1850
milestones.description: Kirkman's puzzle asked for a day-by-day arrangement of fifteen girls in rows of three, adding the requirement that the triples split into parallel classes; the puzzle became far better known than the earlier paper.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia dates the problem to 1850 and the Phil. Mag. solution to 1850
Crossref record of a Kirkman note of 1850 titled 'On the triads made with fifteen things', Phil. Mag. 37, 169-171

milestones.note: The Crossref title and year are matched to the schoolgirl solution by title only; I did not read the note.

milestones.label: Steiner restates triple systems
milestones.work: Steiner, Combinatorische Aufgaben, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 45, 181-182, 1853
milestones.description: Steiner independently posed the triple-system problem, unaware of Kirkman's paper; his version, not Kirkman's, later gave the systems their name.

evidence.claim: Crossref record for Steiner's note, Crelle 45, 181-182
Wikipedia states Steiner published without knowing Kirkman's 1847 paper

milestones.label: Yates introduces incomplete blocks in experimental design
milestones.work: Yates, Incomplete randomized blocks, Annals of Eugenics 7, 121-140, 1936
milestones.description: Yates used designs in which every pair of treatments meets equally often to reduce block size in field experiments, the first statistical use of the combinatorial structure.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of Yates 1936, Ann. Eugenics 7, 121-140

milestones.note: The evidence confirms only the paper, year and title; that this is the earliest statistical use of balanced designs is the standard account but was not checked against a history page.

milestones.label: Witt names the systems after Steiner
milestones.work: Witt, Über Steinersche Systeme, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 12, 265-275 (Crossref year 1937)
milestones.description: The earliest title I found using the name 'Steiner systems'; the volume is dated 1938 in some citations.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of Witt's paper (issued 1937, Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 12, 265-275)

milestones.note: Only the first title found; an earlier use of the name could exist. Crossref gives 1937 online, volume cited as 1938 elsewhere.

milestones.label: Bose's systematic constructions of balanced incomplete block designs
milestones.work: Bose, On the construction of balanced incomplete block designs, Annals of Eugenics 9, 353-399, 1939
milestones.description: A long paper constructing balanced incomplete block designs with finite-geometry and difference methods, linking the statistics to the Kirkman-Steiner tradition.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of Bose 1939, Ann. Eugenics 9, 353-399

milestones.note: Role judged from the title and venue; content not read.

milestones.label: Complete solution of Kirkman's problem
milestones.work: Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson, Solution of Kirkman's schoolgirl problem, Proc. Symp. Pure Math. 19, 187-203, 1971
milestones.description: Existence of a Kirkman triple system for every order congruent to 3 mod 6 was proved in print, completing a problem open since 1850.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of the 1971 paper
Wikipedia says Lu Jiaxi proved the general case first in 1965, but his submission was rejected in error

milestones.note: Priority dispute: Lu Jiaxi (1965, unpublished in time) versus Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson (1971). Denniston 1974 solved Sylvester's related problem.

notes: The summary calls Kirkman's puzzle 'an early case' of designs; sources show the underlying triple-system paper (1847) preceded the 1850 puzzle by three years and Steiner's 1853 restatement. Sylvester claimed in 1861 to have invented the problem and Kirkman rejected the claim (Wikipedia). Michel Reiss 1859 reworked Kirkman's results, and Cole 1922 (Crossref 10.1090/s0002-9904-1922-03599-9) listed all seven solutions; neither is a milestone. Not found: a journal or classification naming 'design theory' and an unambiguous coinage of 'combinatorial designs'. Lifespans of Cummings and Ray-Chaudhuri are from memory and not checked. person without verified work: James Joseph Sylvester (developer).

phases: The abstract concept of a Riemann surface

milestones.label: Puiseux on algebraic functions and branch points
milestones.work: Victor Puiseux, Recherches sur les fonctions algebriques, J. Math. Pures Appl. 15, 1850
milestones.description: Analyses algebraic functions near branch points, the local picture Riemann's surfaces assemble.

evidence.claim: Numdam record: Recherches sur les fonctions algebriques, J. Math. Pures Appl. 15.
Riemann's thesis builds on Cauchy and on Puiseux's ideas of branch points.

milestones.label: Riemann's doctoral dissertation
milestones.work: Riemann, Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse, doctoral thesis, Göttingen, 1851
milestones.description: Riemann's thesis studied analytic functions through geometric surfaces on which many-valued functions become single-valued, introducing topology into complex function theory.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says the thesis studied what we now call Riemann surfaces and was examined on 16 December 1851, building on Puiseux's branch points
MacTutor's topology history says Riemann studied connectivity in 1851 and introduced his surfaces for the equation f(w,z)=0

milestones.note: The thesis was not found in Crossref, zbMATH or Open Library; evidence is a history page. The topology page links the surface introduction to 1857, the biography to the thesis, so the exact date of the first statement is slightly uncertain.

milestones.label: Riemann's theory of Abelian functions
milestones.work: Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 54, 115-155, 1857
milestones.description: Riemann treated many-valued functions as single-valued on a special surface and solved general inversion problems of Abelian integrals, showing the surface concept carried real theorems.

evidence.claim: Crossref record: Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, Crelle 54, 115-155 (1857)
MacTutor says this paper developed the Riemann surface idea and solved inversion problems for Abelian integrals

milestones.label: C. Neumann's lectures on Riemann's theory
milestones.work: Carl Neumann, Vorlesungen ueber Riemann's Theorie der Abel'schen Integrale, Leipzig, 1865
milestones.description: First textbook account of Riemann's surfaces and Abelian integrals.

evidence.claim: Vorlesungen ueber Riemann's Theorie der Abel'schen Integrale, 1865.

milestones.note: 'First textbook' is not checked beyond the title; Neumann's 1884 second edition also exists.

milestones.label: Weyl's book on the idea of a Riemann surface
milestones.work: Weyl, Die Idee der Riemannschen Fläche, Teubner, Leipzig, 1913
milestones.description: Weyl gave a rigorous, abstract definition of a Riemann surface as a manifold with a complex structure, severing it from covering of the plane.

evidence.claim: zbMATH lists Weyl, Die Idee der Riemannschen Fläche (1913)
Internet Archive copy of the 1913 first edition
Wikipedia's article on Riemann surfaces cites Weyl 1913 as the standard foundational text

milestones.note: Klein's 1882 treatment of Riemann's theory is a likely earlier systematic account but was not verified (Crossref shows only the 1923 reprint).

milestones.label: Rado shows Riemann surfaces have countable bases
milestones.work: T. Rado, Ueber den Begriff der Riemannschen Flaeche, Acta Szeged 2, 1925
milestones.description: Settles the abstract definition of a Riemann surface, showing the surfaces are not too large.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record, Acta Szeged 2, 101-121 (1925).

milestones.note: The statement of the result is from memory of the standard account; the zbMATH record confirms title, author and year only.

works.citation: Riemann, Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen, 1851
Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, Crelle 1857

works.citation: Weyl, Die Idee der Riemannschen Fläche, 1913
Recherches sur les fonctions algebriques, J. Math. Pures Appl. 15

works.whyItMatters: First lecture-course exposition of Riemann's theory.

notes: Riemann's thesis (1851) and the 1857 paper are the dated milestones; MacTutor's biography and its topology history differ slightly on which introduced the surfaces. No dated first use of the name 'Riemann surface' was found; naming and institution milestones are open. Klein 1882 and the later triangulation theorem (Rado) were not located in bibliographic databases and are not listed. Puiseux's lifespan is from memory. person without verified work: Victor Puiseux (developer). Added in thin-3 pass: Puiseux 1850 (Numdam), Neumann 1865, Rado 1925. Klein was dropped from people (no verified work found); his 1882 book is part of the later story. Puiseux's lifespan (1820-1883) is from general knowledge; check before use. English Wikipedia's Riemann surface article has no history section, so MacTutor Riemann was the history source. Fix pass 2: an Open Library title search for the 1851 thesis returned no record in this pass, so the thesis year stays without a bibliographic record.

phases: Riemann's use of the minimum principle

milestones.phase: Riemann's use of the minimum principle
milestones.label: Riemann uses the principle in his thesis
milestones.work: Riemann, Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse, doctoral thesis, Göttingen, 1851
milestones.description: Riemann relied on a minimum principle for Dirichlet's integral to guarantee that functions with prescribed boundary behaviour exist, and he is credited with naming it after Dirichlet.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: the name 'Dirichlet's principle' is due to Riemann, who applied it to complex analytic functions and assumed the minimum is attained
MacTutor says the principle was used in Riemann's doctoral thesis and again in 1857

milestones.note: The thesis is also the first application to existence of complex functions, so the same paper plays both roles. The thesis itself is not in the bibliographic databases I searched.

milestones.phase: Riemann's use of the minimum principle
milestones.label: Riemann reuses the principle for Abelian functions
milestones.work: Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, Crelle 54, 115-155, 1857
milestones.description: The principle again underpins the existence results for functions on Riemann surfaces, exposing it to Weierstrass' later criticism.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of the paper
MacTutor says the principle was used again for the results of this 1857 paper

milestones.label: Weierstrass criticises the principle
milestones.work: Weierstrass, Über das sogenannte Dirichlet'sche Princip, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1870
milestones.description: Weierstrass gave a functional whose greatest lower bound is not attained, showing Riemann's assumption that the minimum exists was not justified.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: Weierstrass published the first criticism in 1870 with a functional whose infimum is not attained
Crossref lists reprints of the note (Mathematische Werke, vol. 2, pp. 49-54)

milestones.note: Only reprints are in Crossref; the 1870 year of first publication rests on Wikipedia.

milestones.label: Weber titles a note on Riemann's proof of the Dirichlet principle
milestones.work: Weber, H., A note on Riemann's proof of the Dirichlet principle, 1870
milestones.description: The earliest zbMATH title found that names the Dirichlet principle.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record: title with "Dirichlet principle", Weber, 1870

milestones.note: Earlier titles with Dirichlet principle absent in zbMATH 1850-1869. Riemann's own use in 1857 papers is not a title match.

milestones.label: Hilbert justifies the principle
milestones.work: Hilbert, Über das Dirichlet'sche Princip, 1900; full proof in Mathematische Annalen 59, 161-186, 1904
milestones.description: Hilbert's direct method in the calculus of variations restored the principle under suitable assumptions, answering Weierstrass' objection.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: Hilbert justified Riemann's use in 1900 by the direct method
Crossref record of Hilbert's full treatment in Math. Ann. 59 (1904)
zbMATH 31.0418.01: Hilbert, 'On the Dirichlet principle', Jahresbericht DMV 8 (1900), pp. 184-188.

milestones.note: The 1900 date is from Wikipedia (talk and short paper); the verified publication is 1904. Both dates cited so the milestone stands as a range of about 1900 to 1904.

milestones.label: Kellogg publishes a monograph on potential theory
milestones.work: Kellogg, O. D., Foundations of potential theory, 1929
milestones.description: Monograph covering the variational (Dirichlet) approach to potential problems.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the monograph with first publication year 1929

milestones.note: Monograph chosen as the broad consolidation of potential theory; coverage of the Dirichlet principle not checked page by page.

milestones.phase: Riemann's use of the minimum principle
milestones.label: Earlier uses of the variational principle in potential theory
milestones.work: Gauss, Green and Thomson (Kelvin), earlier work in potential theory
milestones.description: MacTutor notes that Gauss, Green and Thomson had all made use of the minimum principle before Riemann used it for function theory.

evidence.claim: MacTutor's Riemann biography says the principle was not new with Riemann because Gauss, Green and Thomson had used it

milestones.note: Years and works were not identified in the page; searched MacTutor Riemann biography, Wikipedia 'Dirichlet's principle'. Left unknown.

works.citation: Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, Crelle 1857
Weierstrass, Über das sogenannte Dirichlet'sche Princip, 1870

people.name: David Hilbert

works.citation: Hilbert, Über das Dirichletsche Prinzip, Math. Ann. 1904

people.roleNote: repaired it by the direct method

works.citation: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, Vorlesungen über die im umgekehrten Verhältniss des Quadrats der Entfernung wirkenden Kräfte (lectures on potential theory, ed. Grube, 1876)
works.whyItMatters: Dirichlet's lectures on inverse-square potential theory, where the variational principle the record names was taught; the section was not read.

notes: Early uses by Gauss, Green and Thomson are only mentioned in a history page, so the precursor has no year. Riemann's first use of the name 'Dirichlet'sche Princip' in print was not located (naming milestone left open). Courant's 1950 monograph (cited in Wikipedia) is a likely consolidation but 'first systematic treatment' was not checked. Hilbert's 1900 Jahresbericht paper is not in Crossref; Schwarz, Neumann and Poincare alternatives were not searched. person without verified work: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet (popularizer). Fix pass 2: zbMATH confirms Hilbert's 1900 note on the Dirichlet principle (Jahresber. DMV 8, 184-188), which is the 1900 part of the range milestone. Open Library's Courant 1950 book was not added as a milestone in this pass. Fix pass 2: a zbMATH author/year search for Weierstrass 1870 returned no record; only a 1898 Polish translation (JFM 29.0373.06) of 'On the so called Dirichlet principle' is listed, so the 1870 date stays unresolved.

canonicalName: Map colouring and the four colour problem (Kempe and Heawood)

milestones.label: Guthrie's question and De Morgan's letter
milestones.work: De Morgan to Hamilton, 23 October 1852
milestones.description: A student's observation that four colours seem enough for any map reached De Morgan, who asked Hamilton the same day; the letter is the first record of the conjecture.

evidence.claim: MacTutor tells the story of the Guthrie brothers, De Morgan's letter of 23 October 1852 and Hamilton's reply three days later
Wikipedia gives the same first record

milestones.note: Private correspondence, hence a precursor.

milestones.label: Cayley poses the problem in print
milestones.work: Cayley, On the colouring of maps, Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society 1, 259-261, 1879
milestones.description: After asking the London Mathematical Society in June 1878 whether the problem had been solved, Cayley wrote up why it is hard in a note published in 1879.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of Cayley, On the Colouring of Maps (1879)
MacTutor describes the 1878 question to the LMS and the 1879 paper

milestones.note: Earlier printed mentions may exist; I only checked the history pages and Crossref.

milestones.label: Kempe's chain argument
milestones.work: Kempe, On the geographical problem of the four colours, American Journal of Mathematics 2, 193-200, 1879
milestones.description: Kempe announced a proof in Nature in July 1879 and gave it in the American Journal of Mathematics, using chains of alternately coloured regions; the proof was later shown to be flawed.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of Kempe's paper, Am. J. Math. 2, 193
MacTutor explains Kempe's announcement of 17 July 1879 and the method of Kempe chains

milestones.note: The wrong proof is still the origin of the chain method, which Heawood reused.

milestones.label: Heawood refutes Kempe and bounds colours on surfaces
milestones.work: Heawood, Map-colour theorem, Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics 24, 332-338, 1890
milestones.description: Heawood found the gap in Kempe's argument, proved that five colours suffice for the plane and gave a bound for surfaces of higher genus through the Euler characteristic.

evidence.claim: zbMATH lists Heawood, Map-colour theorem, Quart. J. 1890
MacTutor's Heawood biography summarises the five-colour theorem and genus bound of this paper

Heegaard's critique of Betti's definition (no year given) and the 1899 Complément were not examined. The 1847 Listing milestone concerns the field name, not Betti numbers. milestones.phase: Riemann's monodromy viewpoint and Fuchsian equations
milestones.label: Riemann's paper on functions of the Gauss series
milestones.work: Riemann, Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α, β, γ, x) darstellbaren Functionen, Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen 7, 1857
milestones.description: Riemann characterised hypergeometric functions by their behaviour under analytic continuation, the viewpoint Hilbert later said Riemann probably had in mind for the existence problem.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's problem text, as quoted by Wikipedia, says Riemann himself may have had the problem in mind

milestones.note: The link between this particular paper and the problem is my knowledge, not stated on the pages I read; only Hilbert's remark about Riemann and the paper title in the reprint are cited.

The 1895 Schlesinger work and Riemann's 1857 paper are weakly evidenced. Lifespans of Röhrl, Plemelj and Schlesinger are from memory or MacTutor slugs and not rechecked.
